sections.h2: What is a sheriff sale in New Jersey?
sections.html:
A sheriff sale is the public auction that ends a New Jersey mortgage foreclosure. The Superior Court issues a writ of execution after final judgment, and that writ tells the county sheriff to sell the home to the highest bidder. The NJ Courts foreclosure page calls New Jersey a judicial foreclosure state, so every case runs through the Office of Foreclosure or a Superior Court General Equity judge.

Each county sheriff runs its own sales calendar, bidder rules and check-in routine. Morris County, Somerset County and Gloucester County all post their own terms, and the details differ from one county to the next. Ask the sheriff's sales unit in the county where the house sits for the current schedule before you plan around a date.

sections.h2: What has to happen before the sheriff can sell a New Jersey house?
sections.html:
The sheriff cannot list a home until the lender has finished several steps in court. According to the Judiciary's own description, the sequence runs like this:

  • The lender sends a Notice of Intent to Foreclose. The homeowner has 30 days from receipt to pay off the debt or reach another arrangement, and may ask for mediation.
  • The lender files a complaint, and the homeowner has 35 days to answer. No answer within 35 days makes the case uncontested.
  • Before asking for default, the lender gives a final chance to cure 14 days ahead. The homeowner then has 10 days to respond and 45 days to cure or work something out.
  • If the debt is not cured, the court enters final judgment and issues the writ of execution.

The notice of intent must also say that the homeowner can sell or transfer title. That line matters if you would rather sell the house than watch it go to auction.

sections.h2: How long can a New Jersey sheriff sale be delayed?
sections.html:
The sheriff has 150 days from the writ of execution to auction the property. Inside that window the borrower and the lender may each ask for two stays, and a fifth is possible if both sides request it. In some cases a defendant can ask for one more stay to pursue mediation.

County rules add practical detail. Gloucester County says each side gets two adjournments per foreclosure docket, with a written confirmation and a new sale date for the defendant. Morris County takes a Request for Statutory Adjournment form and requires it before noon on the scheduled sale day. A bankruptcy filing generally triggers an automatic stay, and the foreclosure resumes where it stopped once that case is resolved, according to the Judiciary's foreclosure FAQ. The sheriff must also advertise the sale for at least four weeks before holding it.

sections.h2: How do bidders buy at a New Jersey sheriff sale?
sections.html:
Bidding is an open outcry auction with no sealed bids, and the property goes to the highest bidder. The county pages open for this guide agree on the money terms. The winner pays at least 20 percent of the bid at the close of the sale, and the balance is due within 30 days. Interest runs on the balance from the 11th day after the sale, and extra time to arrange a mortgage is not granted.

Opening bids differ by county. Somerset County says the plaintiff opens at $1,000 and later bids rise in multiples of at least $1,000. Morris County and Gloucester County list a minimum bid of $100. Somerset no longer accepts cash for deposits or balances, Morris sets a $1,000 cash limit unless the sheriff approves more, and Gloucester requires a bidder registration form emailed by noon on the Tuesday before the sale.

  • A buyer gets a sheriff's deed once the full balance is paid, and the deed may not carry clear title.
  • Tax, sewer and water liens can follow the property, so the counties urge a title search before bidding.
  • Sales are subject to restrictions of record and to the rights of occupants or tenants.
  • No one may walk through the house beforehand, because the owner has no duty to allow an inspection.

Morris County also describes the Community Wealth Preservation Program. After an August 28, 2025 court order in MER-C-94-24, its right of refusal goes only to defendants, next of kin or tenants, and qualifying participants pay a 3.5 percent deposit.

sections.h2: Can the owner get the house back after the sale?
sections.html:
Yes, for a short time. The homeowner has 10 days after the auction to redeem, which the Judiciary explains as buying the property back or selling it. A successful redemption returns the bidder's deposit. Gloucester County adds that the 10 days can be extended only by a court order, and Somerset County notes that a bankruptcy filed in the same period puts the sale on hold until the court rules.

If nobody redeems, the sale proceeds first pay off the mortgage. Any amount left over returns to the homeowner. When the proceeds fall short, the lender can sue the homeowner for the remaining balance. A homeowner who suspects money is owed after the sale should ask the sheriff and the court clerk about surplus funds, and should be careful with anyone who offers to chase that money for a fee. Gloucester County links a Consumer Affairs fact sheet on surplus funds scams from its sheriff's sale page.

sections.h2: What happens to the people living in the house after a sheriff sale?
sections.html:
Occupants usually stay until some time after the auction. The lender's side must ask the court for a Writ of Possession, which instructs the sheriff to remove anyone still inside, and the sheriff tells the defendant the date to leave. Gloucester County stresses that a winning bidder has no right to enter until the deed is executed and a signed writ of possession is in hand.

Renters get separate protection. The Judiciary says a residential tenant with a valid lease in good standing is not forced to move because of foreclosure, and the buyer at the sheriff sale takes the building subject to the tenant's rights. The state's anti-eviction statute, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, is the law the court points to. A tenant served with a foreclosure complaint should speak to an attorney and can give the lender's lawyer a copy of the lease.

sections.h2: What paperwork and fees come with a sheriff's deed?
sections.html:
Two state forms show up in this process. When the sale is requested, a completed Affidavit of Consideration for Sheriff's Deeds, Form RTF-8, goes to the sheriff. It lists other mortgagees and the balance of prior mortgages and liens, and the Division of Taxation states that it is not an exemption from the Realty Transfer Fee. The second item is the gross income tax withholding form used for deed recording. The Division says only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are excused from signing the seller forms GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

The buyer records the deed with the county clerk and pays those recording fees. Court costs for the foreclosure itself are a lender matter, and the Judiciary lists them as $405 for a complaint, $175 for an answer or first appearance and $50 for a motion.

sections.h2: What can a New Jersey owner do instead of waiting for the sale?
sections.html:
Options exist before and after judgment. A homeowner can reinstate the missed payments, pay the judgment, take a new loan, or sell. New Jersey offers free foreclosure mediation, and the Judiciary advises asking for it as early as possible after receiving the foreclosure notice. A homeowner who qualifies can also look into a hardship stay of the sale through the mediation process.

Be wary of anyone promising a loan modification or foreclosure rescue. The Judiciary names these as scams spreading across New Jersey and recommends a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Because the owner keeps the right to sell until the auction, a quick sale to a buyer who pays off the lender from proceeds can end the case without a sheriff's deed. Ask the lender's attorney for a written payoff figure before you set a closing date.

faqs.q: How many days does a New Jersey homeowner have to redeem after a sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Ten days. The 10 days start with the auction, and the owner can buy the house back or sell it in that window. County sheriffs say only a court order can extend the period.

faqs.q: Does a New Jersey sheriff sale buyer have to pay all cash?
faqs.a: No. The winner pays at least 20 percent when the sale ends and the rest within 30 days, but counties do not grant extra time for a mortgage. Most sheriffs require certified funds, and some set a cash limit or ban cash.

faqs.q: Can a tenant be thrown out after a sheriff sale in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Not on the sale date alone. The NJ Courts say a tenant with a valid lease in good standing keeps tenant rights, and the buyer takes the building subject to them. Removal of an owner occupant needs a Writ of Possession.

faqs.q: Who gets the money left over from a New Jersey sheriff sale?
faqs.a: The homeowner receives what remains after the mortgage debt is paid. If the proceeds do not cover the debt, the lender can sue for the difference.

faqs.q: How long does a sheriff have to sell a house after the writ of execution?
faqs.a: The sheriff has 150 days from the writ. Each side may request two stays and a fifth is possible if both agree, so the real timeline can run longer than the sale date first advertised.
